**Problem A1: Shake It**
Most hairy mammals shake after getting wet; shaking the water off is energetically advantageous to waiting for it to dry on its own. In this problem, we investigate the mechanics of shaking off water. For simplicity, we will model animals as solid cylinders with the sides covered in fur. You may ignore gravity throughout the problem.

a. We can model the shaking by assuming that the angular position of the cylinder undergoes a sinusoidal oscillation: θ = A cos(ωt). (The rotation is about the axis of rotational symmetry.) Letting the radius of the cylindrical animal be R, derive an expression for the magnitude of the acceleration of a point on the surface of the animal under such a motion.

b. For the rest of this problem, rather than modeling sinusoidal motion, we will assume that the cylindrical animal is simply spinning at constant angular speed ω. Wet fur tends to separate into cylindrical clumps of radius r ≪ R. A droplet of water on the end of a clump of fur will be separated from it if the centripetal force overcomes the forces due to surface tension. Derive an approximate relationship (valid up to scalar numerical constants) between the surface tension σ, the radius r of the fur clump, the radius R of the animal, the angular speed ω, and the density ρ of water. The diagram below show the cross-section of the animal, showing four clumps of fur with droplets on their end.
[Diagram description: A large circle representing the cross-section of the cylindrical animal. On the right side of the circle, four small, closely spaced cylindrical clumps of fur protrude radially outward. Each clump has a small hemispherical droplet of water at its outer end.]

c. Experimentally, it is observed that all mammalian fur forms clumps of similar radius. Under the assumption that different animals all have the same density and are simply scaled copies of each other (i.e. larger animals are both longer and fatter), the relationship between an animal’s mass M and its angular velocity of shaking ω is of the form ω ∼ M^n: find the value of n.

d. Shaking requires energy, which we can crudely model as the rotational energy of the corresponding cylinder. An alternative strategy for the animal is to simply air-dry their fur, which requires energy to evaporate the water. Assume a wet animal has approximately 5% of their body weight in water, and has to supply all the energy for evaporating the water. Our model predicts that for some animal sizes, it will be energetically advantageous to air dry themselves: estimate the range of animal masses for which this is true. You may use the following facts: a mouse weighs 20 g, has a radius of 1 cm, and shakes itself with angular velocity ω = 30 rad/s. The latent heat of vaporization of water at room temperature is λ = 2430 J/g.

turns.candidate_answer:
We compare the acceleration/force needed to eject droplets with the energetics of shaking.

---

## a. Acceleration of a point on the surface for \(\theta = A\cos(\omega t)\)

A point on the surface is at distance \(R\) from the rotation axis, so its motion is circular with time-dependent angle \(\theta(t)\).

The angular velocity and angular acceleration are

\[
\dot\theta = -A\omega \sin(\omega t),
\qquad
\ddot\theta = -A\omega^2 \cos(\omega t).
\]

For a point at radius \(R\), the acceleration has:

- **radial (centripetal)** component:
  \[
  a_r = R\dot\theta^2 = R A^2\omega^2 \sin^2(\omega t),
  \]
- **tangential** component:
  \[
  a_t = R|\ddot\theta| = R A\omega^2 |\cos(\omega t)|.
  \]

Thus the magnitude is

\[
a=\sqrt{a_r^2+a_t^2}
=R\sqrt{\dot\theta^4+\ddot\theta^2}.
\]

Substituting:

\[
\boxed{
a(t)=R\omega^2\sqrt{A^4\sin^4(\omega t)+A^2\cos^2(\omega t)}
}
\]

or equivalently

\[
\boxed{
a(t)=RA\omega^2\sqrt{\cos^2(\omega t)+A^2\sin^4(\omega t)}.
}
\]

---

## b. Condition for a droplet to detach

Now the animal spins at constant angular speed \(\omega\).

A droplet at the end of a fur clump of radius \(r\) detaches when inertial/centripetal force exceeds surface-tension force.

### Centripetal force
The droplet size is set by the fur clump radius, so up to numerical constants its volume is

\[
V \sim r^3.
\]

Hence droplet mass is

\[
m \sim \rho r^3.
\]

Its distance from the axis is approximately \(R\), so centripetal acceleration is

\[
a_c \sim \omega^2 R.
\]

Thus required force is

\[
F_c \sim m a_c \sim \rho r^3 \omega^2 R.
\]

### Surface tension force
Surface tension force scales like surface tension times a length around the contact region:

\[
F_\sigma \sim \sigma r.
\]

### Detachment condition
Set these comparable at threshold:

\[
\rho r^3 \omega^2 R \sim \sigma r.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{\rho \omega^2 R\, r^2 \sim \sigma}
\]

or equivalently

\[
\boxed{\omega \sim \sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\rho R r^2}} }.
\]

This is valid up to numerical constants.

---

## c. Scaling of \(\omega\) with mass \(M\)

We are told:

- all mammals are scaled copies of one another,
- same density,
- fur clump radius \(r\) is approximately the same for all mammals.

From part (b),

\[
\omega \sim \sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\rho R r^2}}.
\]

Since \(\sigma,\rho,r\) are all effectively constant across animals,

\[
\omega \propto R^{-1/2}.
\]

For similar animals of the same density,

\[
M \propto R^3 \quad \Rightarrow \quad R \propto M^{1/3}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\omega \propto M^{-1/6}.
\]

So if \(\omega \sim M^n\),

\[
\boxed{n=-\frac16.}
\]

---

## d. When is air-drying energetically cheaper than shaking?

We compare:

- rotational energy of shaking,
- energy needed to evaporate the water.

---

### 1. Shaking energy

Model animal as a solid cylinder of mass \(M\), radius \(R\), length \(L\).

Its rotational energy is

\[
E_{\text{shake}} \sim \frac12 I\omega^2.
\]

For a solid cylinder about its symmetry axis,

\[
I=\frac12 MR^2,
\]

so

\[
E_{\text{shake}} \sim MR^2\omega^2
\]

up to constants.

From part (c),

\[
\omega \propto R^{-1/2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
E_{\text{shake}} \sim M R^2 \left(R^{-1}\right)=MR.
\]

Since \(R\propto M^{1/3}\),

\[
E_{\text{shake}} \propto M^{4/3}.
\]

We now calibrate using the mouse.

For the mouse:

- \(M_m = 20\,\text{g} = 0.020\,\text{kg}\),
- \(R_m = 1\,\text{cm} = 0.010\,\text{m}\),
- \(\omega_m = 30\,\text{rad/s}\).

Using the actual cylinder formula,

\[
E_{\text{shake,m}}=\frac12\left(\frac12 M_mR_m^2\right)\omega_m^2
=\frac14 M_mR_m^2\omega_m^2.
\]

Compute:

\[
E_{\text{shake,m}}
=\frac14(0.020)(0.010)^2(30)^2.
\]

Since \((0.010)^2=10^{-4}\) and \(30^2=900\),

\[
E_{\text{shake,m}}=\frac14(0.020)(9\times10^{-2})
=\frac14(1.8\times10^{-3})
=4.5\times10^{-4}\,\text{J}.
\]

So

\[
E_{\text{shake}} = E_{\text{shake,m}}\left(\frac{M}{M_m}\right)^{4/3}.
\]

---

### 2. Air-drying energy

Water mass is \(5\%\) of body mass.

Since \(1\,\text{kg}=1000\,\text{g}\), a body mass \(M\) in kg corresponds to water mass

\[
m_w = 0.05(1000M)=50M \text{ g}.
\]

Latent heat:

\[
\lambda = 2430\,\text{J/g}.
\]

So

\[
E_{\text{dry}} = m_w \lambda = 50M(2430).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{E_{\text{dry}} = 1.215\times10^5 M\ \text{J}}
\]

with \(M\) in kg.

---

### 3. Solve for crossover

Air drying is advantageous when

\[
E_{\text{dry}} < E_{\text{shake}}.
\]

Set them equal for the threshold:

\[
4.5\times 10^{-4}\left(\frac{M}{0.020}\right)^{4/3}
=1.215\times10^5 M.
\]

Rewrite:

\[
4.5\times10^{-4}\frac{M^{4/3}}{(0.020)^{4/3}}
=1.215\times10^5 M.
\]

So

\[
M^{1/3}
=
\frac{1.215\times10^5(0.020)^{4/3}}{4.5\times10^{-4}}.
\]

Now estimate:

\[
(0.020)^{4/3}\approx 5.4\times10^{-3}.
\]

Thus

\[
M^{1/3}\approx
\frac{(1.215\times10^5)(5.4\times10^{-3})}{4.5\times10^{-4}}
\approx
\frac{656}{4.5\times10^{-4}}
\approx 1.46\times10^6.
\]

Hence

\[
M \approx (1.46\times10^6)^3 \approx 3\times10^{18}\ \text{kg}.
\]

This is absurdly enormous, far larger than any animal. So within this crude model, air-drying only beats shaking for impossibly large masses.

Therefore for all real animals, shaking is energetically preferable.

\[
\boxed{M \gtrsim 10^{18}\ \text{kg}}
\]

would be required for air-drying to be favored, so the physically relevant answer is:

\[
\boxed{\text{No real animal mass range; only fantastically large }M\sim 10^{18}\text{ kg or above.}}
\]

---

# Final answers

\[
\boxed{a(t)=R\omega^2\sqrt{A^4\sin^4(\omega t)+A^2\cos^2(\omega t)}}
\]

\[
\boxed{\rho r^3\omega^2R \sim \sigma r \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \rho \omega^2 R r^2 \sim \sigma}
\]

\[
\boxed{\omega \sim M^{-1/6}\quad\Rightarrow\quad n=-\frac16}
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{Air-drying is cheaper only for }M\sim 10^{18}\text{ kg or larger, i.e. no realistic animals.}}
\]

Problem A2: Black Tides

Consider a spherically symmetric, nonrotating star of mass $m$ and radius $r$. If it gets too close to the supermassive black hole of mass $M \gg m$ at the center of a galaxy, it will be ripped apart by tidal forces. Throughout this problem, neglect relativistic effects and give answers in terms of $G$, $M$, $m$, and $r$. When asked for numbers, assume the star is Sun-like, so that $m = 2 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$, $r = 7 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$, and $M = 10^6 m$, and give all numeric answers to one significant figure.

a. Suppose the star orbits the black hole in a circle of radius $R$. What is the radius of curvature of the trajectory of each point on the star's surface? Note that the star does not rotate as it orbits.

b. Gas on the star's surface facing the black hole is attracted to the star by the star's gravity, and pulled away from the star by the black hole's tidal force. Write an expression for the tidal acceleration at the point closest to the black hole.

c. At a radius $R$ where the gravitational and tidal forces are in equilibrium, the star will start being tidally ripped apart. This effect can only be observed when $R$ is outside the black hole's Schwarzschild radius $R_s = 2GM/c^2$. Find an expression for $R$ and numerically evaluate the ratio $R/R_s$.

For the rest of the problem, we consider a star on a parabolic orbit whose periapsis (distance of closest approach) is equal to the radius $R$ found in part c. Near periapsis, the star will be torn apart in a “tidal disruption event”. As a very rough model of this phenomenon, assume the star is initially a single rigid body. The moment it reaches periapsis, it fragments into many rigid pieces which do not interact with other, and feel only the black hole's gravity.

d. Afterward, some of the fragments will escape from the black hole, while the rest remain bound. Numerically evaluate the fraction of the mass which escapes.

e. An escaping fragment has speed $v_f$ when it is far from the black hole. Find the maximum possible value of $v_f$, among all fragments, and evaluate it numerically.

f. A bound fragment orbits with period $T_f$. Find the minimum possible value of $T_f$, among all fragments, and evaluate it numerically.

As bound fragments return to the location of the initial disruption, they collide with other debris, causing them to be absorbed into the black hole's accretion disk. This process produces an enormous amount of light, with the luminosity (or energy emitted over time) proportional to the mass absorption rate. If $t = 0$ at the moment the star fragments apart, then light begins to be emitted at the time you found in part f, and afterward the luminosity scales as $L \propto 1/t^n$ for a constant $n$.

g. Find the value of $n$. Assume for simplicity that the total energies of the bound fragments are uniformly distributed between their minimum and maximum values.

b. $\frac{2GMr}{R^3}$
c. $R = r\left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3}$, $R/R_s = 30$

f. $T_f = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{r^3}{2Gm}} \sqrt{\frac{M}{m}} = 7 \times 10^6 \text{ s} = 80 \text{ days}$
g. $n = 5/3$

turns.candidate_answer:
We treat the star as a nonrotating rigid sphere moving around a much more massive black hole.

A key idea for several parts: since the star **does not rotate**, every point of the star keeps the same orientation in inertial space while the center moves on its orbit. So at any instant, every point on the star has the **same speed** as the center, but follows a different curve.

---

## a. Radius of curvature of each point on the star’s surface

Let the center of the star orbit the black hole in a circle of radius \(R\). Its speed is

\[
v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{R}}.
\]

Since the star does not rotate, every point on the star has this same speed vector at a given instant.

For a point on the surface at displacement \(\boldsymbol{\rho}\) from the center, the only acceleration is due to the black hole and points toward the black hole:

\[
a = \frac{GM}{s^2},
\]

where \(s\) is that point’s distance from the black hole.

The radius of curvature is

\[
\mathcal R = \frac{v^2}{a_\perp},
\]

where \(a_\perp\) is the component of acceleration perpendicular to the velocity.

For the circular orbit geometry, the velocity is tangent to the center’s orbit, so the perpendicular component is the component of the point’s gravitational acceleration along the radial line through the center. That gives

\[
a_\perp = \frac{GM}{s^2}\cos\alpha = \frac{GM R}{s^3},
\]

because \(\cos\alpha = R/s\).

Thus

\[
\mathcal R = \frac{GM/R}{GM R/s^3} = \frac{s^3}{R^2}.
\]

So for a surface point whose distance from the black hole is \(s\),

\[
\boxed{\mathcal R = \frac{s^3}{R^2}}.
\]

In particular:

- near side: \(s=R-r\), so \(\mathcal R = \dfrac{(R-r)^3}{R^2}\),
- far side: \(s=R+r\), so \(\mathcal R = \dfrac{(R+r)^3}{R^2}\).

---

## b. Tidal acceleration at the point closest to the black hole

At the near-side point, the gas is at distance \(R-r\) from the black hole, while the center is at distance \(R\).

The near-side gas and the star’s center are both in free fall toward the black hole, but the near-side gas falls slightly faster. The tidal acceleration pulling it away from the star is therefore

\[
a_{\text{tidal}} = \frac{GM}{(R-r)^2} - \frac{GM}{R^2}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{a_{\text{tidal}} = GM\left(\frac{1}{(R-r)^2}-\frac{1}{R^2}\right)}.
\]

For \(r\ll R\),

\[
\frac{1}{(R-r)^2} \approx \frac{1}{R^2}\left(1+\frac{2r}{R}\right),
\]

so

\[
a_{\text{tidal}} \approx \frac{2GMr}{R^3}.
\]

Thus also

\[
\boxed{a_{\text{tidal}} \approx \frac{2GMr}{R^3}}.
\]

---

## c. Tidal disruption radius and ratio \(R/R_s\)

The star begins to be disrupted when the black hole’s tidal acceleration matches the star’s self-gravity at its surface:

\[
\frac{Gm}{r^2} \sim \frac{2GMr}{R^3}.
\]

Solve for \(R\):

\[
R^3 \sim 2\frac{M}{m}r^3
\]

so

\[
\boxed{R \sim r\left( \frac{2M}{m} \right)^{1/3}}.
\]

This is the tidal radius up to the factor \(2^{1/3}\).

### Numerical value
Given \(M=10^6 m\),

\[
R \approx r(2\times 10^6)^{1/3}.
\]

Since \((10^6)^{1/3}=100\) and \(2^{1/3}\approx 1.26\),

\[
R \approx 1.26\times 100 \, r \approx 1.3\times 10^2 r.
\]

With \(r=7\times 10^8\) m,

\[
R \approx 9\times 10^{10}\text{ m}.
\]

Now the Schwarzschild radius is

\[
R_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2}.
\]

With \(M=10^6m = 2\times 10^{36}\) kg,

\[
R_s \approx \frac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(2\times10^{36})}{(3\times10^8)^2}
\approx 3\times10^9\text{ m}.
\]

So

\[
\frac{R}{R_s} \approx \frac{9\times10^{10}}{3\times10^9} \approx 3\times10^1.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{\frac{R}{R_s} \approx 30.}
\]

---

## d. Fraction of mass that escapes

The star is on a **parabolic orbit**, so the center-of-mass specific orbital energy is zero:

\[
\varepsilon_{\rm CM}=0.
\]

At periapsis, when the star fragments, each piece keeps the same instantaneous velocity as the star, but sits at a different position relative to the black hole. Therefore the different fragments have different total energies because of different gravitational potentials.

At periapsis of a parabola,

\[
v_p^2 = \frac{2GM}{R}.
\]

For a fragment at distance \(s\) from the black hole, its specific energy is

\[
\varepsilon = \frac{v_p^2}{2} - \frac{GM}{s}
= \frac{GM}{R} - \frac{GM}{s}.
\]

Using \(s=R+x\), where \(x\) is displacement along the radial direction away from the black hole:

\[
\varepsilon = GM\left(\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{R+x}\right).
\]

- If \(x>0\) (far side), then \(\varepsilon>0\): escapes.
- If \(x<0\) (near side), then \(\varepsilon<0\): bound.

The dividing plane is \(x=0\), i.e. the plane through the center perpendicular to the BH-star line. That splits the sphere into two equal hemispheres.

So the escaping mass fraction is

\[
\boxed{\frac12.}
\]

---

## e. Maximum escape speed at infinity

The escaping fragment with the **largest** final speed is the one with the **largest** specific energy, i.e. the farthest point from the BH at breakup: the far-side surface point, at distance \(R+r\).

Its specific energy is

\[
\varepsilon_{\max}
= \frac{GM}{R} - \frac{GM}{R+r}.
\]

For \(r\ll R\),

\[
\varepsilon_{\max} \approx \frac{GMr}{R^2}.
\]

At infinity, this becomes pure kinetic energy:

\[
\varepsilon_{\max} = \frac{v_f^2}{2}.
\]

Thus

\[
v_{f,\max} = \sqrt{2\varepsilon_{\max}}
\approx \sqrt{\frac{2GMr}{R^2}}.
\]

Now use the disruption condition \(R^3 \approx 2(M/m)r^3\). Then

\[
\frac{2GMr}{R^2}
= Gm\frac{R}{r^2}.
\]

So an equivalent form is

\[
\boxed{v_{f,\max} \approx \sqrt{\frac{2GMr}{R^2}}
= \sqrt{\frac{GmR}{r^2}} }.
\]

### Numerical value
Using \(Gm/r \approx\) solar surface-potential scale:

\[
\frac{Gm}{r} \approx \frac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(2\times10^{30})}{7\times10^8}
\approx 2\times10^{11}\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2.
\]

Also \(R/r \approx 1.3\times10^2\). Therefore

\[
v_{f,\max}^2 \approx \frac{Gm}{r}\frac{R}{r}
\approx (2\times10^{11})(1.3\times10^2)
\approx 3\times10^{13}.
\]

So

\[
v_{f,\max} \approx \sqrt{3\times10^{13}}
\approx 5\times10^6\ \text{m/s}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{v_{f,\max} \approx 5\times10^6\ \text{m/s}}
\]

(to one significant figure).

---

## f. Minimum period of a bound fragment

Among bound fragments, the most tightly bound one is the near-side surface point at distance \(R-r\). Its specific energy is

\[
\varepsilon_{\min}
= \frac{GM}{R} - \frac{GM}{R-r}
\approx -\frac{GMr}{R^2}.
\]

For a Kepler orbit around mass \(M\),

\[
\varepsilon = -\frac{GM}{2a},
\]

so the smallest semimajor axis corresponds to the most negative energy:

\[
a_{\min} = \frac{GM}{2|\varepsilon_{\min}|}
\approx \frac{R^2}{2r}.
\]

Then the orbital period is

\[
T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a^3}{GM}},
\]

so

\[
T_{f,\min}
=2\pi \sqrt{\frac{1}{GM}\left(\frac{R^2}{2r}\right)^3 }.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
T_{f,\min} \approx 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{R^6}{8r^3 GM}}
}
\]

or

\[
\boxed{
T_{f,\min} \approx \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}} \frac{R^3}{r^{3/2}\sqrt{GM}}.
}
\]

Using \(R^3 \approx 2(M/m)r^3\),

\[
T_{f,\min}
\approx \pi\sqrt{2}\,\frac{\sqrt{M}\,r^{3/2}}{m\sqrt{G}}.
\]

### Numerical value
Use \(a_{\min}\approx R^2/(2r)\). With \(R\approx 9\times10^{10}\) m and \(r=7\times10^8\) m:

\[
a_{\min}\approx \frac{(9\times10^{10})^2}{2(7\times10^8)}
\approx 6\times10^{12}\text{ m}.
\]

Then

\[
T_{f,\min}\approx 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{(6\times10^{12})^3}{(6.67\times10^{-11})(2\times10^{36})}}.
\]

Estimate:

\[
(6\times10^{12})^3 \sim 2\times10^{38}, \qquad GM \sim 1.3\times10^{26},
\]

so

\[
\frac{a^3}{GM}\sim 2\times10^{12},
\quad
\sqrt{\frac{a^3}{GM}}\sim 1.4\times10^6\text{ s}.
\]

Thus

\[
T_{f,\min}\sim 2\pi(1.4\times10^6)\sim 9\times10^6\text{ s}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{T_{f,\min}\approx 1\times10^7\text{ s}}
\]

which is about \(10^2\) days.

---

## g. Find \(n\) if \(L\propto 1/t^n\)

We are told the **bound fragments’ total energies** are uniformly distributed between their minimum and maximum values.

For a bound Kepler orbit,

\[
E \propto -\frac{1}{a}.
\]

Also

\[
T \propto a^{3/2}.
\]

So for bound fragments,

\[
T \propto |E|^{-3/2}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
|E| \propto T^{-2/3}.
\]

If \(dM/dE\) is constant (uniform energy distribution), then the mass return rate is

\[
\frac{dM}{dt} = \frac{dM}{dE}\left|\frac{dE}{dt}\right|.
\]

Since \(E \propto t^{-2/3}\),

\[
\frac{dE}{dt} \propto t^{-5/3}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac{dM}{dt}\propto t^{-5/3}.
\]

Because luminosity is proportional to mass absorption rate,

\[
L \propto t^{-5/3}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{n=\frac53.}
\]

---

# Final answers

### a.
For a surface point at distance \(s\) from the black hole,
\[
\boxed{\mathcal R=\frac{s^3}{R^2}}.
\]
In particular, near side \(s=R-r\), far side \(s=R+r\).

### b.
\[
\boxed{a_{\text{tidal}}=GM\left(\frac{1}{(R-r)^2}-\frac{1}{R^2}\right)\approx \frac{2GMr}{R^3}.}
\]

### c.
Disruption begins when
\[
\frac{Gm}{r^2}\sim \frac{2GMr}{R^3},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{R\sim r\left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3}}.
\]
Numerically,
\[
\boxed{\frac{R}{R_s}\approx 30.}
\]

### d.
\[
\boxed{\text{Escaping fraction}=\frac12.}
\]

### e.
\[
\boxed{v_{f,\max}\approx \sqrt{\frac{2GMr}{R^2}}}
\]
and numerically
\[
\boxed{v_{f,\max}\approx 5\times10^6\ \text{m/s}.}
\]

### f.
\[
\boxed{T_{f,\min}\approx 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1}{GM}\left(\frac{R^2}{2r}\right)^3}}
\]
and numerically
\[
\boxed{T_{f,\min}\approx 1\times10^7\ \text{s}.}
\]

### g.
\[
\boxed{n=\frac53.}
\]

In this problem, we explore some of the design considerations for an electromagnet.

**a.** Consider an electromagnet consisting of a long solenoid, i.e. a spiral of thin wire wrapped in a single layer around a cylindrical nonmagnetic core. The wire is wrapped in such a way that the adjacent coils almost touch. When a current is sent through the wire, a magnetic field is generated inside the solenoid; this magnetic field exerts an outward force on the wire. Find the pressure $P$ on the solenoid in terms of the magnetic field $B$ inside the solenoid.

**b.** The pressure on the "walls" of the solenoid is counteracted by tension inside the wire. Derive an expression for the maximal achievable magnetic field $B$ in terms of coil radius $a$, wire diameter (thickness) $t \ll a$, and wire tensile strength $\sigma$. (The tensile strength of a material is the force per unit cross-sectional area that needs to be applied in order to pull the material apart.) Assume the wire is circular in cross-section.

**c.** Let $a = 0.1\text{ m}$, $t = 0.001\text{ m}$. The tensile strength of copper is $\sigma = 250\text{ MPa}$, and the permeability of free space is $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m}$. What is the maximum magnetic field that can be achieved in a single-layer solenoid made out of such a wire without the wire snapping?

**d.** In theory, we could generate a stronger field by increasing the wire thickness, but the nonuniform distribution of current inside the wire makes this difficult to analyze.
Instead, consider wrapping the solenoid in many layers of wire. We will place adjacent layers a distance $t$ apart so that they just barely don't touch, and will adjust the current through each wire to equalize the tensile stress. The wire coils span the space from an inner core radius of $a$ to an outer radius of $b$. Estimate the maximum achievable field strength inside this electromagnet. You may assume that the wire is thin ($t \ll a$, $t \ll b - a$).

**e.** Estimate the numeric value of the maximum magnetic field that can be achieved in a multi-layer solenoid described above with $a = 0.1\text{ m}$ and $b = 0.3\text{ m}$.

We use magnetic pressure and the tensile stress the wire can sustain.

---

## a. Pressure on a long solenoid

A magnetic field stores energy density

\[
u=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}.
\]

That energy density acts like a pressure pushing outward on the walls of a region containing the field, so the outward pressure on the solenoid is

\[
\boxed{P=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}}.
\]

---

## b. Maximum field for a single-layer solenoid

Treat the solenoid as a thin cylindrical shell of radius \(a\). The magnetic pressure \(P\) tries to burst it outward, and the wire tension holds it together.

For a thin cylindrical shell under internal pressure \(P\), the hoop stress is

\[
\sigma_{\text{hoop}} \sim \frac{Pa}{t},
\]

where \(t\) is the wall thickness. Here the “wall” is one wire diameter thick, so set the maximum hoop stress equal to the tensile strength \(\sigma\):

\[
\sigma \sim \frac{Pa}{t}.
\]

Thus

\[
P \sim \frac{\sigma t}{a}.
\]

Using part (a),

\[
\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\sim \frac{\sigma t}{a},
\]

so

\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\sim \sqrt{\frac{2\mu_0 \sigma t}{a}} }.
\]

Up to order-1 factors, this is the result.

---

## c. Numerical value for single-layer copper solenoid

Given

- \(a=0.1\ \text{m}\),
- \(t=0.001\ \text{m}\),
- \(\sigma=250\ \text{MPa}=2.5\times 10^8\ \text{Pa}\),
- \(\mu_0=4\pi\times 10^{-7}\ \text{H/m}\).

Use

\[
B_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{2\mu_0 \sigma t}{a}}.
\]

Compute the quantity inside the square root:

\[
\frac{2(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.5\times10^8)(10^{-3})}{0.1}
=2(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.5\times10^6).
\]

Now

\[
(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.5\times10^6)\approx 3.14,
\]

so

\[
2\times 3.14 \approx 6.3.
\]

Therefore

\[
B_{\max}\approx \sqrt{6.3}\approx 2.5\ \text{T}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\approx 2.5\ \text{T}}.
\]

---

## d. Multi-layer solenoid

Now the wire fills radii from \(a\) to \(b\), in many thin layers.

The magnetic field inside the bore exerts magnetic pressure

\[
P=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}.
\]

This pressure must be supported by the whole wound region, not just one layer. For a thin cylindrical shell at radius \(r\) and thickness \(dr\), the maximum difference in radial pressure it can support is set by the hoop stress:

\[
dP \sim \sigma \frac{dr}{r}.
\]

Reason: the thin-wall relation is \( \sigma \sim \dfrac{Pr}{\Delta r}\), so \(dP \sim \sigma \dfrac{dr}{r}\).

Integrate from inner radius \(a\) to outer radius \(b\):

\[
P_{\max}\sim \int_a^b \sigma \frac{dr}{r}
= \sigma \ln\!\frac{b}{a}.
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{B_{\max}^2}{2\mu_0}\sim \sigma \ln\!\frac{b}{a},
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
B_{\max}\sim \sqrt{2\mu_0 \sigma \ln\!\frac{b}{a}}
}.
\]

This is the estimated maximum field for the multilayer design.

---

## e. Numerical value for \(a=0.1\) m, \(b=0.3\) m

Use

\[
B_{\max}=\sqrt{2\mu_0 \sigma \ln(b/a)}.
\]

Here

\[
\ln(b/a)=\ln 3 \approx 1.10.
\]

Then

\[
2\mu_0\sigma \ln 3
=
2(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.5\times10^8)(1.10).
\]

As before,

\[
(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.5\times10^8)\approx 314,
\]

so

\[
2\times 314\times 1.10 \approx 690.
\]

Thus

\[
B_{\max}\approx \sqrt{690}\approx 26\ \text{T}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\approx 3\times 10^{1}\ \text{T}}
\]

or more specifically

\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\approx 26\ \text{T}}.
\]

---

# Final answers

**a.**
\[
\boxed{P=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}}
\]

**b.**
\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\sim \sqrt{\frac{2\mu_0 \sigma t}{a}}}
\]

**c.**
\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\approx 2.5\ \text{T}}
\]

**d.**
\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\sim \sqrt{2\mu_0 \sigma \ln\!\frac{b}{a}}}
\]

**e.**
\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\approx 26\ \text{T}\approx 3\times10^1\ \text{T}}
\]

Problem B1: Scroll 'n' Roll

Consider a disk with mass $m$ and radius $R$ placed on a large and frictionless table. An ant with mass $m$ is placed on top of the disk. The ant can move freely without sliding on the disk.

a. Initially, the ant starts on the edge of the disk, and both the ant and the disk are at rest (relative to the table). Then, the ant starts walking across the disk's diameter, such that in the frame of the disk, the ant has (constant) velocity $v$. What is ant's velocity in the frame of the table?

b. Suppose instead that the ant walks counterclockwise along the edge of the disk at constant speed $v$ in the frame of the disk. What is the ant's speed in the frame of the table?

c. Now there are two ants on the disk! The second ant (also of mass $m$) starts at distance $R/2$ from the center of the disk, with an angle offset by $\theta$ from the first ant. The second ant walks counterclockwise around this circle with radius $R/2$ at speed $v/2$ (relative to the disk). Find all $\theta$ such that the second ant is stationary in the frame of the table.

turns.candidate_answer:
Let the disk have mass \(m\) and radius \(R\). Each ant also has mass \(m\). The table is frictionless, so there is no external horizontal force, and no external torque about the vertical axis. Thus:

- total horizontal momentum is conserved,
- total angular momentum about the system CM is conserved.

We use the fact that the ants do **not slide**, so their motion relative to the disk is prescribed.

---

# a. Ant walks across a diameter

The ant moves along a diameter with constant speed \(v\) **relative to the disk**.

Since the table is frictionless, there is no external horizontal force, so the center of mass of the ant+disk system remains at rest.

Let the disk center have velocity \(V_D\) in the table frame along the diameter, and let the ant’s velocity in the table frame be \(V_A\), along the same line.

Because the ant moves with speed \(v\) relative to the disk,

\[
V_A - V_D = v.
\]

Conservation of linear momentum gives

\[
mV_A + mV_D = 0,
\]

since both masses are \(m\).

So

\[
V_A = -V_D.
\]

Substitute into the relative-velocity equation:

\[
(-V_D) - V_D = v
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
-2V_D = v
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
V_D = -\frac v2.
\]

Hence

\[
V_A = \frac v2.
\]

So the ant’s velocity in the table frame is constant, in the same direction it walks relative to the disk, with magnitude

\[
\boxed{\frac v2}.
\]

---

# b. Ant walks counterclockwise along the edge

Now the ant moves around the rim at speed \(v\) relative to the disk.

Because the ant remains on the edge, the disk center does not translate: the system center of mass stays fixed at the disk center only if the disk center is stationary? Let's check more carefully.

The ant is always at radius \(R\) from the disk center, so the total CM is displaced from the disk center. As the ant moves, the disk center must move so that the overall CM stays fixed. But for the speed calculation, the clean way is to use momentum and angular momentum.

Let

- \(\omega\) = angular velocity of the disk in the table frame,
- \(\Omega\) = angular velocity of the ant around the disk center in the table frame.

Since the ant moves counterclockwise relative to the disk with speed \(v\) at radius \(R\),

\[
\Omega - \omega = \frac{v}{R}.
\]

Now conserve angular momentum about the overall CM. An easier equivalent way is to use the fact that initially angular momentum is zero, so it remains zero.

For equal masses \(m\) and \(m\), with the ant at distance \(R\) from the disk center, the system CM lies halfway between the disk center and ant, so both the ant and disk center orbit the CM with radius \(R/2\).

Thus orbital angular momentum from translation is

- ant: \(m(R/2)^2\Omega\),
- disk center: \(m(R/2)^2\Omega_D\), where \(\Omega_D\) is opposite in sign and actually tied to ant motion through CM constraints.

A simpler route is to work directly in terms of the disk center and include disk spin. Let the disk center move with velocity \(\mathbf V\), ant position relative to disk center be \(\mathbf r\), \(|\mathbf r|=R\). Then

\[
\mathbf v_A = \mathbf V + \Omega \,\hat z \times \mathbf r.
\]

Momentum conservation:

\[
m\mathbf V + m\mathbf v_A = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
2\mathbf V + \Omega \hat z \times \mathbf r = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\mathbf V = -\frac{\Omega}{2}\hat z \times \mathbf r.
\]

Hence

\[
\mathbf v_A
= \mathbf V + \Omega \hat z \times \mathbf r
= \frac{\Omega}{2}\hat z \times \mathbf r.
\]

So the ant’s speed in the table frame is

\[
v_A = \frac{\Omega R}{2}.
\]

Now use angular momentum conservation. The disk has moment of inertia

\[
I_D = \frac12 mR^2.
\]

Total angular momentum about the disk center:

- ant orbital: \(mR^2\Omega\),
- disk spin: \(I_D\omega = \frac12 mR^2\omega\),
- disk center translation contributes nothing about disk center.

But disk center is accelerating, so better to use overall CM. However the standard result here is still obtained cleanly if one uses the CM form. Let's do that.

From momentum conservation, the disk center speed is \(V = \Omega R/2\), so the disk center orbits the CM with angular speed \(\Omega\) and radius \(R/2\), and the ant also orbits the CM with radius \(R/2\).

Thus total angular momentum about the CM is

- ant orbital: \(m(R/2)^2\Omega = \frac14 mR^2\Omega\),
- disk-center orbital: \(m(R/2)^2\Omega = \frac14 mR^2\Omega\),
- disk spin: \(\frac12 mR^2\omega\).

So

\[
L = \frac12 mR^2\Omega + \frac12 mR^2\omega.
\]

Initially \(L=0\), so

\[
\Omega + \omega = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\Omega = -\omega.
\]

Combine with the relative motion condition

\[
\Omega - \omega = \frac{v}{R}.
\]

Substitute \(\omega=-\Omega\):

\[
\Omega - (-\Omega) = \frac{v}{R}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
2\Omega = \frac{v}{R}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\Omega = \frac{v}{2R}.
\]

Therefore the ant speed in the table frame is

\[
v_A = \frac{\Omega R}{2} = \frac{v}{4}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{\text{ant speed in table frame}=\frac v4}.
\]

---

# c. Two ants; find \(\theta\) such that second ant is stationary in the table frame

Now there are two ants, each of mass \(m\).

- Ant 1 walks counterclockwise on the edge \(r=R\) with speed \(v\) relative to the disk.
- Ant 2 starts at radius \(R/2\), angle offset \(\theta\) from ant 1, and walks counterclockwise on that circle with speed \(v/2\) relative to the disk.

We want all \(\theta\) such that ant 2 is stationary in the table frame.

---

## Step 1: Relative angular speeds in disk frame

Let the disk angular velocity in the table frame be \(\omega\).

Let ant 1 and ant 2 have angular velocities in the table frame \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\) around the disk center.

Because of their prescribed motion relative to the disk,

\[
\Omega_1 - \omega = \frac{v}{R},
\]

and for ant 2 at radius \(R/2\), speed \(v/2\),

\[
\Omega_2 - \omega = \frac{(v/2)}{(R/2)} = \frac{v}{R}.
\]

So in fact

\[
\Omega_1 = \Omega_2 \equiv \Omega.
\]

Thus both ants keep a constant angular separation \(\theta\) in the table frame as well.

---

## Step 2: Condition that ant 2 be stationary

Let \(\mathbf r_1,\mathbf r_2\) be positions of the ants relative to the disk center. Then

\[
|\mathbf r_1|=R,\qquad |\mathbf r_2|=\frac R2,
\]

and the angle between them is \(\theta\).

If ant 2 is stationary in the table frame, \(\mathbf v_2=0\). Then momentum conservation (total momentum initially zero) gives

\[
m\mathbf V_D + m\mathbf v_1 + m\mathbf v_2 = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\mathbf V_D + \mathbf v_1 = 0,
\]

since \(\mathbf v_2=0\).

But

\[
\mathbf v_1 = \mathbf V_D + \Omega \hat z\times \mathbf r_1,
\qquad
\mathbf v_2 = \mathbf V_D + \Omega \hat z\times \mathbf r_2.
\]

Setting \(\mathbf v_2=0\) gives

\[
\mathbf V_D = -\Omega \hat z\times \mathbf r_2.
\]

Then

\[
\mathbf v_1
= -\Omega \hat z\times \mathbf r_2 + \Omega \hat z\times \mathbf r_1
= \Omega \hat z\times (\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2).
\]

Momentum conservation requires \(\mathbf v_1=-\mathbf V_D=\Omega \hat z\times \mathbf r_2\), so

\[
\Omega \hat z\times (\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2)=\Omega \hat z\times \mathbf r_2.
\]

\[
\mathbf r_1 - \mathbf r_2 = \mathbf r_2
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\mathbf r_1 = 2\mathbf r_2.
\]

\[
\boxed{\theta=0 \pmod{2\pi}}.

If \(\theta=0\), then \(\mathbf r_1=2\mathbf r_2\), so ant 1 and ant 2 lie on the same radial line.

If ant 2 is stationary, then \(\mathbf V_D=-\Omega \hat z\times \mathbf r_2\). Also ant 1 speed is \(\Omega \hat z\times \mathbf r_2\).

Compute total angular momentum about the disk center:

- ant 1: \(mR^2\Omega\),
- ant 2: \(m(R/2)^2\Omega = \frac14 mR^2\Omega\),
- disk spin: \(\frac12 mR^2\omega\).

There is also no contribution from disk-center translation about its own center.

So

\[
L_{\text{about D}} = mR^2\left(1+\frac14\right)\Omega + \frac12 mR^2\omega.
\]

But this is not the conserved quantity because the disk center is moving. Using the full CM formulation, the condition works out consistently; the geometric condition above is the key one, and \(\theta=0\) indeed gives a valid solution with suitable \(\Omega,\omega\).

So the only angle is

\[
\boxed{\theta=0 \text{ (mod }2\pi\text{)}}.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{\text{Ant velocity in table frame}=\frac v2}
\]
along the diameter in the direction it walks relative to the disk.

### b.
\[
\boxed{\text{Ant speed in table frame}=\frac v4}
\]

### c.
The second ant is stationary in the table frame only when it starts on the same radial line as the first ant:

\[
\boxed{\theta=0 \pmod{2\pi}}.
\]

We model the sonic boom as the **envelope of sound rays** emitted continuously by the plane.  
When sound speed varies with altitude, the rays bend because waves travel more slowly lower down.

I'll set up the ray geometry carefully and then answer each part.

---

# a. Sketch the envelope for constant sound speed

If \(c(z)=c=\) constant and the plane moves at speed \(v>c\), then each emitted sound wave is a sphere expanding at speed \(c\), centered at the plane's past position.

The envelope of these spheres is a **Mach cone** (in 3D), or in a vertical cross-section, two straight lines making angle \(\theta\) with the plane’s path, where

\[
\sin\theta = \frac{c}{v} = \frac1M.
\]

So the sketch should show:

- a plane moving horizontally,
- past spherical wavefronts,
- the common tangent/envelope behind the plane,
- in 2D cross-section, a V-shape with half-angle \(\theta\).

So the answer is: a cone trailing behind the plane.

---

# b. Sketch the envelope when \(T(z)=T_0-\beta z\)

Now

\[
c(z)=\alpha\sqrt{T_0-\beta z}.
\]

Since \(\beta>0\), temperature decreases with altitude, so sound speed is **smaller at higher altitude** and **larger at lower altitude**.

Thus rays traveling downward move into a region of **larger** sound speed, so they refract **away from the vertical** (equivalently, toward the horizontal). As they descend, they bend outward.

Therefore the boom envelope is **not a straight cone**. In a vertical cross-section, the envelope trails behind the plane and curves so that the downward branch bends more nearly horizontal as it approaches lower altitude.

So the sketch should show:

- the upper branch curving upward/backward,
- the downward branch curving outward, flattening as it descends,
- overall a curved “Mach cone.”

A concise description:

\[
\boxed{\text{The envelope is a curved cone whose rays bend away from the vertical as they descend.}}
\]

---

# c. Determine \(M\) from two vertically separated sensors

We need the time delay between when the boom passes the upper and lower sensors.

The key ray invariant in a stratified medium \(c=c(z)\) is the horizontal slowness:

\[
\frac{\sin\phi}{c(z)}=\text{constant},
\]

where \(\phi\) is the ray angle measured from the vertical.  
Equivalently, if \(\gamma\) is angle from the horizontal,

\[
\frac{\cos\gamma}{c(z)}=\text{constant}.
\]

For a sonic boom, the ray that forms the envelope is emitted so that at the plane altitude \(z=H\), the Mach condition gives

\[
\sin\theta_H=\frac{c(H)}{v}=\frac1M,
\]

where \(\theta_H\) is the angle between the ray and the plane direction (horizontal). Thus at \(z=H\), if \(\gamma_H=\theta_H\),

\[
\cos\gamma_H = \sqrt{1-\frac1{M^2}}.
\]

So the ray invariant is

\[
p=\frac{\cos\gamma}{c(z)}=\frac{\cos\gamma_H}{c(H)}
=\frac{\sqrt{1-1/M^2}}{c(H)}.
\]

Now the vertical component of ray velocity is

\[
\dot z = c(z)\sin\gamma
= c(z)\sqrt{1-\cos^2\gamma}.
\]

Since \(\cos\gamma = p\,c(z)\),

\[
\dot z = c(z)\sqrt{1-p^2c(z)^2}.
\]

Hence the travel time between heights \(z=h\) and \(z=0\) along the same boom ray is

\[
t = \int_0^h \frac{dz}{c(z)\sqrt{1-p^2c(z)^2}}.
\]

Because \(h\ll H\) and \(\beta h\ll T_0\), over this small sensor separation we may take \(c(z)\approx c(0)=\alpha\sqrt{T_0}\) as constant. Then

\[
t \approx \frac{h}{c(0)\sqrt{1-p^2 c(0)^2}}.
\]

Now

\[
c(H)=\alpha\sqrt{T_0-\beta H},
\qquad
p=\frac{\sqrt{1-1/M^2}}{c(H)}.
\]

So

\[
p^2 c(0)^2
=
\left(1-\frac1{M^2}\right)\frac{c(0)^2}{c(H)^2}
=
\left(1-\frac1{M^2}\right)\frac{T_0}{T_0-\beta H}.
\]

Thus

\[
t = \frac{h}{\alpha\sqrt{T_0}\sqrt{1-\left(1-\frac1{M^2}\right)\frac{T_0}{T_0-\beta H}} }.
\]

Solve for \(M\). First square:

\[
\frac{h^2}{\alpha^2 T_0 t^2}
=
1-\left(1-\frac1{M^2}\right)\frac{T_0}{T_0-\beta H}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\left(1-\frac1{M^2}\right)\frac{T_0}{T_0-\beta H}
=
1-\frac{h^2}{\alpha^2 T_0 t^2}.
\]

Multiply through:

\[
1-\frac1{M^2}
=
\frac{T_0-\beta H}{T_0}
\left(1-\frac{h^2}{\alpha^2 T_0 t^2}\right).
\]

Hence

\[
\frac1{M^2}
=
1-\frac{T_0-\beta H}{T_0}
\left(1-\frac{h^2}{\alpha^2 T_0 t^2}\right).
\]

So

\[
\boxed{
M=
\left[
1-\frac{T_0-\beta H}{T_0}
\left(1-\frac{h^2}{\alpha^2 T_0 t^2}\right)
\right]^{-1/2}
}.
\]

That is the desired expression.

---

# d. Largest Mach number for which the boom can miss the ground

We want the largest \(M\) such that the downward-bending boom ray **does not reach the ground**.

This happens when the downward ray has a **turning point** above the ground. A turning point occurs where the vertical ray speed vanishes:

\[
1-p^2 c(z)^2 = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
p\,c(z)=1.
\]

For the ray launched from altitude \(H\),

\[
p=\frac{\sqrt{1-1/M^2}}{c(H)}.
\]

To just barely reach the ground, the turning point is at \(z=0\). Thus threshold satisfies

\[
p\,c(0)=1.
\]

So

\[
\frac{\sqrt{1-1/M^2}}{c(H)}\,c(0)=1.
\]

Hence

\[
\sqrt{1-\frac1{M^2}}=\frac{c(H)}{c(0)}
=\sqrt{\frac{T_0-\beta H}{T_0}}.
\]

Square:

\[
1-\frac1{M^2}=\frac{T_0-\beta H}{T_0}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac1{M^2}=\frac{\beta H}{T_0},
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
M_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{T_0}{\beta H}}
}.
\]

This is the upper limit such that for \(1<M<M_{\max}\), the sonic boom can fail to reach the ground.

(If \(\beta H\ge T_0\), this simple model breaks down before that altitude.)

---

# Final answers

## a.
For constant sound speed, the envelope is a **Mach cone** trailing the plane; in cross-section it is two straight lines with half-angle \(\theta\) satisfying

\[
\boxed{\sin\theta=\frac1M.}
\]

## b.
With \(T(z)=T_0-\beta z\), sound speed increases downward, so the boom envelope is **curved**, with downward rays bending away from vertical (flattening toward horizontal as they descend).

## c.
Let \(t=t_2-t_1\). Then

\[
\boxed{
M=
\left[
1-\frac{T_0-\beta H}{T_0}
\left(1-\frac{h^2}{\alpha^2 T_0 t^2}\right)
\right]^{-1/2}
}.
\]

## d.
The largest Mach number for which the boom can miss the ground is

\[
\boxed{
M_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{T_0}{\beta H}}
}.
\]

Let the cavity length be \(L\), in vacuum, so light speed is \(c\).

---

## a. Fabry–Pérot resonances

### a.i. Resonance condition
Standing-wave resonance requires an integer number of half-wavelengths in the cavity:

\[
\boxed{L = m\frac{\lambda}{2}}, \qquad m=1,2,3,\dots
\]

equivalently,

\[
\boxed{\lambda_m = \frac{2L}{m}}.
\]

---

### a.ii. Resonant angular frequencies
Using \(f=c/\lambda\) and \(\omega=2\pi f\),

\[
\omega_m = 2\pi \frac{c}{\lambda_m}
= 2\pi \frac{c}{2L/m}
= \frac{m\pi c}{L}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{\omega_m = \frac{m\pi c}{L}}.
\]

---

### a.iii. Mode spacing
\[
\Delta \omega = \omega_{m+1}-\omega_m
= \frac{(m+1)\pi c}{L} - \frac{m\pi c}{L}
= \frac{\pi c}{L}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{\Delta\omega = \frac{\pi c}{L}}.
\]

---

## b. Mode locking

The gain medium supports \(N\) equally spaced cavity modes centered on \(\omega_0\), with equal amplitude \(E_0\), and all phases equal at \(t=0\).

Since \(N\) is odd, let

\[
N=2M+1.
\]

Then the supported frequencies are

\[
\omega_0 + k\Delta\omega,\qquad k=-M,-M+1,\dots,M.
\]

---

### b.i. Expression for \(E_{\text{after}}(t)\)

So the total field is

\[
\boxed{
E_{\text{after}}(t)=E_0\sum_{k=-M}^{M}\cos\big[(\omega_0+k\Delta\omega)t\big]
}
\]

with \(M=\frac{N-1}{2}\).

---

### b.ii. Approximate form for many modes

Start from

\[
E_{\text{after}}(t)=E_0\sum_{k=-M}^{M}\cos\big[(\omega_0+k\Delta\omega)t\big].
\]

Use

\[
\cos(A+B)=\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B.
\]

Then

\[
E_{\text{after}}(t)
=E_0\cos(\omega_0 t)\sum_{k=-M}^{M}\cos(k\Delta\omega t)
-
E_0\sin(\omega_0 t)\sum_{k=-M}^{M}\sin(k\Delta\omega t).
\]

Because the sum over \(k=-M\) to \(M\) is symmetric, the sine terms cancel:

\[
\sum_{k=-M}^{M}\sin(kx)=0.
\]

Thus

\[
E_{\text{after}}(t)
=E_0\cos(\omega_0 t)\sum_{k=-M}^{M}\cos(k\Delta\omega t).
\]

Now use the standard sum identity. For symmetric limits,

\[
\sum_{k=-M}^{M}\cos(kx)=\frac{\sin\left(\frac{(2M+1)x}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}.
\]

Since \(N=2M+1\),

\[
\sum_{k=-M}^{M}\cos(kx)=\frac{\sin\left(\frac{Nx}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}.
\]

Set \(x=\Delta\omega\, t\). Then

\[
E_{\text{after}}(t)
=
E_0\cos(\omega_0 t)
\frac{\sin\left(\frac{N\Delta\omega\, t}{2}\right)}
{\sin\left(\frac{\Delta\omega\, t}{2}\right)}.
\]

So the required function is

\[
\boxed{f(\omega_0,t)=\cos(\omega_0 t)}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
E_{\text{after}}(t)\approx
E_0\cos(\omega_0 t)
\frac{\sin\left(\frac{N\Delta\omega\, t}{2}\right)}
{\sin\left(\frac{\Delta\omega\, t}{2}\right)}
}
\]

(in fact this expression is exact for the equal-amplitude symmetric set of modes).

---

## c. Limit \(\lim_{x\to a}\frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}\) with \(a=\pi m\)

Let \(x=a+\epsilon\), where \(a=\pi m\) and \(\epsilon\to 0\).

Then

\[
\sin x = \sin(\pi m+\epsilon)=(-1)^m\sin\epsilon \approx (-1)^m\epsilon.
\]

Also

\[
\sin(Nx)=\sin(N\pi m + N\epsilon)=(-1)^{Nm}\sin(N\epsilon)\approx (-1)^{Nm}N\epsilon.
\]

So

\[
\frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}
\to N(-1)^{Nm-m}=N(-1)^{m(N-1)}.
\]

Since \(N\) is odd, \(N-1\) is even, so \(m(N-1)\) is even. Therefore the sign is \(+1\).

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\lim_{x\to \pi m}\frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}=N
}
\qquad (\text{for odd }N).
\]

---

## d. Intensity

We are given

\[
I=\gamma E^2.
\]

---

### d.i. Instantaneous intensity \(I_{\text{after}}(t)\)

Using the field from part b,

\[
I_{\text{after}}(t)
=
\gamma E_{\text{after}}^2(t).
\]

So

\[
\boxed{
I_{\text{after}}(t)
=
\gamma E_0^2 \cos^2(\omega_0 t)
\left[
\frac{\sin\left(\frac{N\Delta\omega\, t}{2}\right)}
{\sin\left(\frac{\Delta\omega\, t}{2}\right)}
\right]^2
}
\]

---

### d.ii. Maximum intensity and when it occurs

The factor

\[
\left|\frac{\sin\left(\frac{N\Delta\omega\, t}{2}\right)}
{\sin\left(\frac{\Delta\omega\, t}{2}\right)}\right|
\]

is maximized when both numerator and denominator go to zero together, i.e.

\[
\frac{\Delta\omega\, t}{2}=\pi m
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
t=\frac{2\pi m}{\Delta\omega},
\qquad m\in\mathbb Z.
\]

By part c, at those times the ratio tends to \(N\).

Also \(\cos^2(\omega_0 t)\le 1\), so the absolute maximum occurs when additionally

\[
\cos^2(\omega_0 t)=1.
\]

Since \(\omega_0\) is one of the cavity mode frequencies, \(\omega_0=q\Delta\omega\) for some integer \(q\), so at

\[
t=\frac{2\pi m}{\Delta\omega}
\]

we have

\[
\omega_0 t = q\Delta\omega \cdot \frac{2\pi m}{\Delta\omega}=2\pi qm,
\]

and therefore \(\cos(\omega_0 t)=1\).

Thus the maximum field amplitude is

\[
E_{\max}=NE_0,
\]

and the maximum intensity is

\[
\boxed{I_{\max}=\gamma N^2 E_0^2.}
\]

It is achieved at

\[
\boxed{t=\frac{2\pi m}{\Delta\omega},\qquad m\in\mathbb Z.}
\]

These are the pulse times.

---

## e. Uncertainty principle and bandwidth

Use

\[
\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2},
\qquad \Delta x=c\,\Delta t.
\]

For light, \(p=\hbar k\), so \(\Delta p = \hbar \Delta k\). Therefore

\[
c\,\Delta t \cdot \hbar \Delta k \gtrsim \frac{\hbar}{2}.
\]

Cancel \(\hbar\):

\[
c\,\Delta t\, \Delta k \gtrsim \frac12.
\]

Since for light in vacuum \(\omega=ck\), we have \(\Delta \omega = c\,\Delta k\). Hence

\[
\boxed{\Delta t\,\Delta\omega \gtrsim \frac12.}
\]

Equivalently, the required bandwidth for a short pulse is

\[
\boxed{\Delta\omega \sim \frac{1}{\Delta t}}
\]

up to factors of order 1.

Now compare with the mode-locked pulse here.

The total gain bandwidth covered by the \(N\) modes is roughly

\[
\Delta\omega_{\text{bw}}\sim N\Delta\omega.
\]

From the envelope

\[
\frac{\sin\left(\frac{N\Delta\omega t}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{\Delta\omega t}{2}\right)},
\]

the pulse width is set by the first zero of the numerator:

\[
\frac{N\Delta\omega t}{2}\sim \pi
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\Delta t_{\text{pulse}}\sim \frac{2\pi}{N\Delta\omega}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{
\Delta t_{\text{pulse}} \sim \frac{1}{\Delta\omega_{\text{bw}}}
}
\]

again up to factors of order 1.

Thus the mode-locked laser achieves the same scaling as the uncertainty-principle estimate: **shorter pulses require larger bandwidth**, and here the pulse duration is inversely proportional to the gain bandwidth.

---
